title: Remarks by Chief Justice Alexander G. Gesmundo at the Book Launch of With Due Respect 3
primary_topics: Remarks by incumbent CJ Alexander G. Gesmundo at the book launch of 'With Due Respect 3' on December 7, 2021 -- CJP's 85th birthday -- published on cjpanganiban.com as a companion piece to SC025

CJ Gesmundo's argument: the case of CJP disproves the life-tenure argument for SC justices -- one can be more prolific and productive outside the Court than within it, validating fixed-tenure retirement at 70
CJP characterized as 'the best argument to a lifetime tenure for Justices' who has mastered 'the Art of Relevance' through his column, his advocacy and his diverse post-retirement involvements
CJ Gesmundo's own reform agenda for the judiciary: efficiency, innovation and access -- and CJP's column as a 'potent aid' in championing this agenda
sub_topics: The JBC interview question: CJ Gesmundo was asked during his JBC interview whether he favored extending SC justices' term beyond 70 (perhaps lifetime tenure like in the US); he immediately answered 'No -- at a certain point productivity wanes' but concedes he may have spoken too soon given CJP's example
CJP as the best counter-argument: at 85, 15 years after retirement, 'looking younger than ever, still spry and vigorous, and very, very relevant'

CJP's biographical outline by Gesmundo: self-made man; public school system; FEU AA and LLB; 1960 bar exam 6th place; mentored by Jovito Salonga; multi-dimensional career (PCCI, PPCRV, World Tourism Organization, MAP, Rotary Club of Manila); Honorary Consul of Honduras; only Filipino Vatican appointee by Pope John Paul II to the Pontifical Council for the Laity; 10 years as Associate Justice + CJ from December 20, 2005; more than 1,000 ponencias (Gesmundo says 1,000+ while CJP himself says 1,200+ in other speeches)
The 'Art of Relevance' -- Gesmundo suggests CJP use this as his next book title: CJP has mastered it through his writing and diverse post-retirement involvements

WDR column's unique role: discusses burning legal issues 'with more freedom than he had when... sitting in the Court bound by its rules and proscriptions'; 'articulates sentiments and views which incumbent members of the Court could only wish to say themselves'

Column's coverage: legal issues of the day; jurisprudential analysis ('incisive and can cut to the quick'); reform advocacy; featuring judiciary reformists (ADR mechanisms, court management techniques, judicial education breakthroughs); always with 'utmost respect for the Court and its rules'

CJ Gesmundo's reform targets: efficiency, innovation and access; guiding principles: timely and fair, transparent and accountable, equal and inclusive, propelled by adaptive management; target -- 5 years for Filipinos to be 'served justice real time, when they need it'

CJP's October 31, 2021 column quote: 'Modesty aside, I was happy at my tenure in the Court. And yet a yearning throbbed deep in my heart that I have not done enough...' -- Gesmundo's response: 'The work is never finished. Whether we work until 70, 80, or until our Creator calls us, we would still regret not having done more.'

Fixed-tenure argument revisited: by hanging robes at 70, the institution assures continuity and revitalization through 'a continuous stream of justices' -- the institution survives technological advancements, pandemics through infusion of new blood
CJP framed as 'our unofficial resident amicus curiae'
Final tribute: thanks CJP for paving the road for 6 Chief Justices after him; looks forward to WDR4 or 'The Art of Relevance'
signature_phrases: retired Chief Justice Artemio Panganiban is proving to be the best argument to a lifetime tenure for Justices of the High Court
Irrelevance, inconsequence, insignificance -- the dreaded curse accompanying retirement
articulates sentiments and views which incumbent members of the Court could only wish to say themselves
incisive and can cut to the quick, but always insightful
I may have spoken too soon
the institution is revitalized... through a continuous stream of justices brought about by a steady retirement

stances.claim: CJP disproves the life-tenure argument for SC justices -- not by demonstrating that justices should serve longer, but by showing that one can be 'more prolific and more productive even outside the Court.' Fixed retirement at 70 assures institutional continuity and revitalization through a steady stream of new justices; prolonged tenure would merely perpetuate individuals at the cost of institutional renewal.
stances.rhetorical_move: paradoxical-proof: CJP's productivity-in-retirement used as an argument FOR fixed tenure and AGAINST the life-tenure position that CJP's example seems to support
stances.confidence: asserted as CJ Gesmundo's institutional reasoning

stances.claim: The greatest accomplishment of CJP's post-retirement career -- more than his directorships or FLP -- is his mastery of 'the Art of Relevance': remaining a 'resonant voice, not just heard but read and listened to by many, from people with no legal background, to lawyers and law students, justices and judges alike, and even those of us currently sitting in the High Court.'
stances.rhetorical_move: relevance-as-supreme-post-retirement-achievement: reframes the dreaded 'curse of retirement' as a challenge CJP has uniquely defeated
stances.confidence: asserted as CJ Gesmundo's personal assessment

stances.claim: CJP's column serves a function that incumbent justices cannot perform -- articulating 'sentiments and views which incumbent members of the Court could only wish to say themselves' -- making the retired CJ an informal but institutionally useful voice of judicial reform advocacy.
stances.rhetorical_move: institutional-utility argument for the retired justice's column: the very freedom from Court constraints that makes the column possible makes it valuable to the Court
stances.confidence: asserted by the incumbent CJ as a frank assessment of the column's function

notable_anecdotes: The JBC interview: when asked during his Chief Justice interview whether SC justices' term should be extended beyond 70, Gesmundo immediately said 'No -- at a certain point in life, the productivity of a person wanes.' He then concedes, looking at CJP at 85: 'I may have spoken too soon.'

The dreaded curse of retirement: 'From the highest position in one of only 3 branches of government, from being number 5 in terms of protocol plate number, hitting 70 ushers in a veritable downgrading to what has been described as a shockingly quiet, unremarked, even obscure existence. But not for Chief Justice Art.'
The 'Art of Relevance' book title suggestion: 'Chief Justice Art has mastered the Art of Relevance. I suggest you use this as the title of your next book, Chief Justice Art.'

The October 31, 2021 column quote and Gesmundo's response: CJP wrote that 'a yearning throbbed deep in my heart that I have not done enough.' Gesmundo: 'It is a surprise that the Chief Justice who wrote a thousand decisions and several books is talking about not having done enough... The work is never finished.'

one_paragraph_summary: Published December 7, 2021 on cjpanganiban.com as a companion to SC025, these are CJ Alexander G. Gesmundo's remarks at the book launch of 'With Due Respect 3' on CJP's 85th birthday. Gesmundo opens with a personal disclosure: when the JBC asked during his CJ interview whether justices' terms should extend beyond 70 (like US lifetime tenure), he immediately said no -- 'at a certain point in life, the productivity of a person wanes.' Looking at CJP at 85, he admits: 'I may have spoken too soon.' He then deploys CJP's example as a paradoxical proof: CJP is 'proving to be the best argument to a lifetime tenure for Justices' -- yet Gesmundo uses this as an argument for fixed retirement, not against it, because 'one can be more prolific and more productive even outside the Court,' and fixed tenure assures institutional renewal through 'a continuous stream of justices.' He presents a concise biographical sketch: self-made man, FEU, 6th in 1960 bar, Salonga-mentored, multi-dimensional career, over 1,000 ponencias, and 15 years of post-retirement relevance. He identifies CJP's 'most influential and potent tool for remaining relevant' as the WDR column -- which discusses burning legal issues 'with more freedom than he had when sitting in the Court... articulating sentiments and views which incumbent members of the Court could only wish to say themselves.' He articulates his own reform agenda -- efficiency, innovation and access on the guiding principles of timely-and-fair, transparent-and-accountable, equal-and-inclusive, adaptive management -- and invites CJP's column as a 'potent aid' in championing it. He responds to CJP's October 31, 2021 confession of not having done enough: 'The work is never finished.' He closes by suggesting CJP's next book title: 'The Art of Relevance,' and thanking him as 'our unofficial resident amicus curiae.'
